lit.'<p>Las rocas cambian de un tipo a otro:
'

Rocks change from one type to another in the rock cycle: weathering and erosion break any rock into sediment; sediment is compacted into sedimentary rock; heat and pressure turn it metamorphic; if it melts it forms magma, which cools into igneous rock. It is driven by the Earth’s internal heat (tectonics) and the Sun’s energy (water, wind, ice).

'
lit.'<p>Las rocas se clasifican por su <b>or:
'

Rocks are classified by their origin. Igneous rocks form when magma cools: slowly at depth (granite, with large crystals) or quickly at the surface (basalt). Sedimentary rocks form when sediments are compacted and cemented (sandstone, limestone) and may contain fossils. Metamorphic rocks are transformed by heat and pressure without melting (marble, gneiss).

'
lit.'<p>Los movimientos tectónicos <b>levant:
'

Tectonic movements lift and sometimes fold or tilt the strata, which formed on the seabed; that is why marine fossils are found in mountains, even in the Andes. Then erosion by rivers and glaciers carves valleys and canyons that expose the sequence of layers, like a book of Earth’s history.

'
lit.'<p>Por el <b>principio de superposición:
'

By the principle of superposition, in undisturbed strata the lower ones are older than those above. A magma intrusion (dyke) is younger than the layers it cuts through. Index fossils (such as trilobites or ammonites), which lived for a short time in many places, allow layers at different sites to be correlated and dated.

'
lit.'<p>Ríos, viento y mar transportan sedim:
'

Rivers, wind and sea carry sediments that settle in horizontal layers at the bottom of lakes and seas. Under the weight of the layers above they are compacted and cemented: strata form. Each stratum records the environment of its time: beach sand, mud from calm waters, plant remains in swamps or shells in warm seas.

'
lit.'<p>Un <b>fósil</b> se forma cuando un o:
'

A fossil forms when an organism dies and is buried quickly by sediment, away from oxygen and decomposers. Over time, hard parts (bones, shells, teeth) are replaced by minerals or leave a mould. Footprints, burrows and droppings are fossils too. Most living things are not fossilised: the fossil record is incomplete.

'
